title: Clamp a glue-up in a wooden handscrew by turning both of its screws so the jaws bear flat along the joint
instruction: Clamp the two glued boards together in the wooden handscrew and leave the clamp holding them.
context: Gluing two boards face to face, or a split part back together, and clamping it while the glue sets is a common home woodworking and furniture-repair job, and the wooden handscrew is a classic clamp for it. A handscrew has two screws, and each sets the opening only at its own point along the jaws. Not stated: turn only the middle handle and the tips pinch the front of the boards while the back gapes; turn only the end handle and the jaws close behind the boards; turn both equally and, because both screws sit behind the work, the jaws end out of parallel, bearing only on the back edge. The robot must watch the gaps at both ends of the jaws and finish each screw by its own amount. Unlike clamping boards with a one-hand bar clamp, or setting bar clamps alternately above and below a panel, where each clamp has one screw or trigger and closes square by itself, this tests coordinating two screws on one clamp until its jaws lie flat.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left). Two dark wooden strips, fixed, 3.8 cm tall, from x 23 to 53: one 5 cm wide from y 2.4 to 7.4, one 6 cm wide from y -2 to -8. Handscrew (10 in wooden handscrew, 1.24 kg in all): two maple jaws 25.4 x 4.4 x 4.4 cm, 0.34 kg each, lying flat along x, one on each strip, tips forward at x 50.7, heels at x 25.3; inner faces at y 2.3 (left jaw) and y -2.3 (right jaw), so they start parallel and 4.6 cm apart. Two steel spindles, 16 mm, run across both jaws along y, 6 cm above the table: the middle spindle at x 38 (12.7 cm behind the tips) and the end spindle at x 28.5. The middle spindle's handle comes out of the left jaw and the end spindle's out of the right jaw: each a wooden handle 3.2 cm wide and 11.5 cm long with a dark stripe along it, on a short steel ferrule, from y 7.1 to 18.6 (left) and y -7.1 to -18.6 (right); with its spindle, 0.28 kg. Each spindle sets the opening only at its own point (left- and right-hand threads): one turn of its handle, clockwise seen from the handle's end, closes the jaws 6 mm there, and the jaws stay straight, so the opening along them follows a straight line through the openings at the two spindles; turning one handle alone tilts the right jaw. The screws hold where they are left and are never turned back by the load. Jaw and board faces have a friction coefficient of 0.5. The jaws and nuts give 1 mm at each spindle per 200 N; past 300 N at a spindle the screw slips. Boards: one maple (pale) and one cherry (red-brown), each 20 x 8.9 x 1.9 cm (3/4 x 3 1/2 in stock), 0.24 kg, standing on edge on the table between the strips with their glued faces together and ends flush, from x 39.2 to 59.2; maple on the left (y 0 to 1.9), cherry on the right (y -1.9 to 0). The jaws cover the boards from 3.8 to 8.2 cm above the table over the first 11.5 cm of their length; the rest sticks out past the tips.
scoring: Measured at the end with a 0.5 mm feeler gauge, a protractor, a ruler, a 4.5 kg weight and a photo. Gaps are measured between each jaw's inner face and the board against it, and between the two boards (the glue line), at the jaw's mid-height, at the boards' end nearest the middle spindle and at the jaw tips. Held: with the clamp lifted by its jaws and a 4.5 kg weight hung from the boards, neither board slips (ruler). The simulation computes this lift test from the modelled screws: their squeeze on the boards is at least 50 N, which at the faces' friction of 0.5 carries the boards plus 4.6 kg. 0 if at any point the clamp was moved more than 3 cm or tilted more than 10 degrees, or a board tipped more than 30 degrees. Otherwise: 1.0 if the jaws are parallel within 0.5 degrees, both bear flat on the boards and the glue line is closed (the gauge enters at neither end of either jaw or of the glue line, and neither end of a jaw is pressed 0.5 mm or more into a board), the boards are held, upright (within 10 degrees) and flush (ends and top edges within 2 mm of each other), both grippers are at least 3 cm from every part of the clamp, and boards and clamp are still (moving less than 1 mm over the last second), all held for 1 s; 0.5 if both jaws touch the boards (somewhere along each jaw the gauge does not enter) and the boards are held and upright, but another 1.0 condition fails; 0.25 if both jaws touch the boards; else 0. Jaws closed behind the boards touch neither board and score 0.
reset_notes: Loosen both handles, take the boards out, set the jaws parallel 46 mm apart at both screws, lay the clamp on the two strips in its marked outline with the handles pointing left and right, and stand the two boards, faces together and ends flush, between the strips inside the jaws.
fidelity: Real size and mass (254 mm maple jaws, 1.24 kg clamp; 3/4 x 3 1/2 in boards). Threads and swivel nuts are not modelled: each control step the two handle angles set stiff drives holding the right jaw (a carriage and a pivot), 6 mm of closing per turn at each spindle (an estimate), self-locking. The handles turn with the same small effort however tight the clamp is, unlike a real screw. Glue is not simulated. Rigid boxes and cylinders; the strips are fixed.
